question: What is the minimum age a candidate must be when applying for a Utah real estate license (sales agent or broker)?
explanation: The Utah Division of Real Estate's licensing requirements state that all applicants must be at least eighteen (18) years of age when they apply for licensure.
source_note: Utah Real Estate Candidate Handbook (Pearson VUE, administered for the Utah Division of Real Estate), 'State Licensing Requirements,' Requirement A: Age, July 2024/rev. 01/2026

question: What formal education must every applicant for a Utah real estate license already possess before applying?
choice_a: An associate's degree in any field
choice_c: No formal education is required at any level
choice_d: A high school diploma, GED, or equivalent as determined by the Utah Real Estate Commission
explanation: Utah licensing requirements provide that all applicants shall have at least a high school diploma, GED, or equivalent as determined by the Utah Real Estate Commission.
source_note: Utah Real Estate Candidate Handbook (Pearson VUE, administered for the Utah Division of Real Estate), 'State Licensing Requirements,' Requirement B: Formal Education

question: How many total classroom hours of prelicensing education must a candidate for a Utah real estate broker license complete?
explanation: Broker candidates must complete one hundred twenty (120) classroom hours of broker prelicensing education, the same total required of salesperson candidates (though the course content differs).
source_note: Utah Real Estate Candidate Handbook (Pearson VUE, administered for the Utah Division of Real Estate), 'State Licensing Requirements,' Requirement C: Prelicensing Education

question: On the Utah Division of Real Estate's Candidate Education Certifying Document, the 120-hour broker prelicensing curriculum is broken into three components. How many hours are allotted to 'Utah Law'?
explanation: The Section B (Broker) breakdown on the Candidate Education Certifying Document allocates 45 hours to Broker Principles, 45 hours to Broker Practices, and 30 hours to Utah Law, for a total of 120 hours.
source_note: Utah Division of Real Estate, Candidate Education Certifying Document, Form 0945-14 (01/23), Section B: Broker

question: What must a candidate present at the test center each time they take a Utah real estate licensing examination, verifying completion of prelicensing education requirements?
choice_a: A notarized letter from their sponsoring broker
choice_b: A copy of their high school diploma
explanation: The Candidate Education Certifying Document, completed by a certified real estate school (and/or by the Division waiving all or part of the requirement), must be presented at the test center every time the exam is taken.
source_note: Utah Real Estate Candidate Handbook (Pearson VUE, administered for the Utah Division of Real Estate), 'State Licensing Requirements,' Requirement C: Prelicensing Education

question: An applicant requests an education waiver from the Utah Division of Real Estate for prelicensing coursework completed in another state. How long must the applicant allow for the Division to review and respond to the submitted documentation?
explanation: Applicants requesting an out-of-state education waiver must submit valid documentation to the Division, and must allow at least thirty (30) days for the Division to review and respond.
source_note: Utah Real Estate Candidate Handbook (Pearson VUE, administered for the Utah Division of Real Estate), 'State Licensing Requirements,' Requirement D: Education Waiver

question: Under Utah's education waiver provisions, which individuals may have their prelicensing education requirement waived simply by providing proof of their membership status?
choice_a: Active members of the Utah State Bar Association
choice_c: Members of the National Association of REALTORS®
explanation: Active members of the Utah State Bar Association may have their prelicensing education waived by providing proof of their membership status; the number of hours waived is indicated on the Candidate Education Certifying Document.
source_note: Utah Real Estate Candidate Handbook (Pearson VUE, administered for the Utah Division of Real Estate), 'State Licensing Requirements,' Requirement D: Education Waiver

question: A candidate completes broker prelicensing education on March 1. By what date must the candidate complete both the examination and the entire licensing process, absent an approved waiver?
choice_a: Within 90 days, i.e., by roughly May 30
choice_b: Within 1 year of the education completion date, i.e., by roughly March 1 of the following year
choice_c: Within 6 months, i.e., by roughly September 1
choice_d: Within 2 years, i.e., by roughly March 1 two years later
explanation: Prelicensing education is good for one (1) year; the candidate must complete the examination and the entire licensing process within one year of the education completion date shown on the Candidate Education Certifying Document.
source_note: Utah Division of Real Estate, Candidate Education Certifying Document, Form 0945-14 (01/23); Utah Real Estate Candidate Handbook, Requirement C: Prelicensing Education

question: After passing both components (general and state) of the Utah real estate licensing examination, within how many days must an applicant submit the proper application forms and fees to the Utah Division of Real Estate?
explanation: All applicants must apply for a license within ninety (90) days of passing both examination components (general and state) and within twelve (12) months of completing prelicensing education.
source_note: Utah Real Estate Candidate Handbook (Pearson VUE, administered for the Utah Division of Real Estate), 'State Licensing Requirements,' Requirement G: Applying for a License and Licensing Deadlines

question: If the 90th day following an applicant's passing examination falls on a Saturday, Sunday, or national holiday, when is the latest the applicant may submit a Utah license application?
choice_a: The application deadline is forfeited entirely and the exam must be retaken
choice_c: The deadline is automatically extended by 30 additional days
explanation: If the 90th day following the examination falls on a weekend or national holiday, the next business day is the latest an applicant may apply for a license.
source_note: Utah Real Estate Candidate Handbook (Pearson VUE, administered for the Utah Division of Real Estate), 'State Licensing Requirements,' Requirement G: Applying for a License and Licensing Deadlines

question: An applicant passes the Utah real estate exam but fails to submit a license application within the required 90-day window. What is the required remedy?
choice_a: The applicant must retake the examination
choice_b: The applicant must retake the entire prelicensing education course only
choice_c: The applicant is permanently barred from Utah licensure
choice_d: The Division automatically issues the license late with a penalty fee
explanation: Applicants who fail to meet the 90-day examination-to-application deadline must retake the examination. (Separately, those who fail to meet the 12-month education deadline must retake the prelicense education, and those who miss both deadlines must retake both.)
source_note: Utah Real Estate Candidate Handbook (Pearson VUE, administered for the Utah Division of Real Estate), 'State Licensing Requirements,' Requirement G: Applying for a License and Licensing Deadlines

question: On the Utah real estate licensing exam, a candidate passes the general portion but fails the state law portion. Within what period may the candidate retake only the failed portion before being required to retake the entire examination?
explanation: The Utah exam is divided into a general and a state law part. A candidate who passes one part and fails the other need retake only the failed section within six (6) months; if both sections are not passed within six months, the candidate must retake the entire examination.
source_note: Utah Real Estate Candidate Handbook (Pearson VUE, administered for the Utah Division of Real Estate), 'Exam Day,' Retaking the Exam

question: After failing a Utah real estate licensing examination, how soon may a candidate make a reservation to retake it?
choice_a: Immediately, at the test center before leaving
explanation: Reservations for reexamination may not be made at the test center, and candidates must wait twenty-four (24) hours after failing an examination before making a reservation to retake it.
source_note: Utah Real Estate Candidate Handbook (Pearson VUE, administered for the Utah Division of Real Estate), 'Exam Day,' Retaking the Exam

question: What scaled passing score must a candidate achieve on each portion (general and state) of the Utah real estate broker examination?
explanation: The Utah Division of Real Estate, in conjunction with Pearson VUE, set the broker examination's passing scaled score at 75 on both the general and state portions (the salesperson passing score is 70 on both portions). Scaled scores range from 0 to 100.
source_note: Utah Real Estate Candidate Handbook (Pearson VUE, administered for the Utah Division of Real Estate), 'Exam Day,' Score Explanation, Passing Scaled Scores table

question: How many scored items appear on the Utah Real Estate State Broker Licensing Examination (the Utah-specific law and rules portion)?
explanation: The Utah broker state-law examination content outline specifies 90 scored items, plus 5-10 additional unscored pretest items. (The Utah salesperson state-law exam, by comparison, has 50 scored items.)
source_note: Utah Real Estate State Broker Licensing Examination Content Outline, Utah Laws, Rules, and Regulations, effective July 15, 2016 (Pearson VUE/Utah Division of Real Estate)

question: Under Utah real estate licensing law, a person who negotiates or arranges even a single real estate transaction in exchange for compensation, without holding a license, has generally violated the licensing requirement under which principle tested on the exam?
explanation: Utah's licensing framework treats even a single compensated act of brokering as sufficient to trigger the license requirement; this 'one act for compensation' concept is listed as a distinct basic definition underlying the requirement that a license is needed to practice real estate in Utah.
source_note: Utah Real Estate State Broker Licensing Examination Content Outline, Utah Laws, Rules, and Regulations, effective July 15, 2016, Section I.C 'One act for compensation' and Section II.A 'License required to practice real estate'

question: What does the acronym 'RELMS,' referenced throughout Utah's license maintenance rules, stand for?
choice_b: Regional Estate Licensing and Monitoring Service
explanation: RELMS is the Real Estate License Management System, the Utah Division of Real Estate's online system used for license renewals, transfers, terminations, activation/inactivation, and tracking continuing education.
source_note: Utah Real Estate State Broker Licensing Examination Content Outline, effective July 15, 2016, Section II.C 'License maintenance — Real Estate License Management System (RELMS)'; Utah Department of Real Estate Continuing Education Provider FAQ, Pearson VUE, Stock #0945-13 (07/22)

question: Which entity is responsible for managing and enforcing continuing education (CE) compliance for Utah real estate licensees?
choice_d: The Utah Division of Real Estate
explanation: Per the Division's own continuing education FAQ, Pearson VUE does not manage CE compliance — the Utah Division of Real Estate manages and enforces all CE compliance, with course credits reported to the Division daily.
source_note: Utah Department of Real Estate Continuing Education Provider FAQ, Pearson VUE, Stock #0945-13 (07/22), Section 'CE Compliance,' Q1.1

question: Where can a Utah real estate agent view their official continuing education transcript?
choice_a: By logging into their account on realestate.utah.gov and selecting RELMS
choice_b: Through the Clarus roster-submission website used by CE providers
choice_c: By calling Pearson VUE customer service
choice_d: CE transcripts are mailed annually and cannot be viewed online
explanation: Agents must set up an account on the Division's website, www.realestate.utah.gov, and select RELMS to view their continuing education transcript. (The Clarus roster site is used by CE providers to report completed courses, not by agents to view transcripts.)
source_note: Utah Department of Real Estate Continuing Education Provider FAQ, Pearson VUE, Stock #0945-13 (07/22), Section 'CE Compliance,' Q1.2

question: Under the reporting requirements tested on the Utah broker exam, an 'Event Occurrence' report that a licensee must file with the Division includes which of the following?
choice_a: A change in the licensee's favorite MLS search filters
choice_b: A criminal conviction or a change in the licensee's contact information
choice_c: A change in the licensee's preferred title company
explanation: The content outline's Reporting Requirements category identifies 'Event Occurrence' reporting as covering, among other things, a criminal conviction and a change in contact information.
source_note: Utah Real Estate State Broker Licensing Examination Content Outline, effective July 15, 2016, Section II.D 'Reporting Requirements — Event Occurrence: Criminal conviction; Contact information; Other'

question: During the Utah licensing exam's qualifying/background questions, a candidate is asked whether they have ever been convicted of, or pled guilty or nolo contendere to, a felony or a class A or class B misdemeanor. According to the candidate handbook, does this disclosure requirement extend to traffic offenses?
choice_a: No, traffic offenses of any kind are always excluded
choice_b: Only felony-level traffic offenses must be disclosed; misdemeanor traffic offenses never need to be disclosed
choice_c: Yes, if the traffic offense was prosecuted as a felony, class A misdemeanor, class B misdemeanor, or comparable criminal offense, disclosure is required
choice_d: Traffic offenses only need to be disclosed if they occurred within the last 12 months
explanation: The handbook's qualifying questions expressly note that a traffic offense can be prosecuted as a felony, class A misdemeanor, class B misdemeanor, or comparable criminal offense, and where that is the case, disclosure is required.
source_note: Utah Real Estate Candidate Handbook (Pearson VUE, administered for the Utah Division of Real Estate), 'Exam Day,' Qualifying Questions #9-10

question: What is the stated consequence of giving a false or inaccurate answer to one of the licensure qualifying questions asked at the Utah exam (e.g., regarding prior disciplinary history)?
choice_a: No consequence, as long as the exam itself is passed
choice_c: A mandatory retake of the general exam portion only
choice_d: License denial, revocation, or other disciplinary action
explanation: The candidate handbook warns candidates to carefully and accurately answer the qualifying questions, because false or inaccurate answers may result in license denial, revocation, or other disciplinary action.
source_note: Utah Real Estate Candidate Handbook (Pearson VUE, administered for the Utah Division of Real Estate), 'Exam Day,' Qualifying Questions

question: Among the licensure qualifying questions, candidates must disclose whether they have ever been sanctioned or banned from engaging in any activity by certain federally related housing/lending organizations. Which organizations are specifically named?
choice_a: Freddie Mac, Fannie Mae, FHA (HUD), and VA
explanation: One of the qualifying questions asks whether the candidate has ever been sanctioned or banned from engaging in any activity by Freddie Mac, Fannie Mae, FHA (HUD), VA, or a similar organization, for any period or reason.
source_note: Utah Real Estate Candidate Handbook (Pearson VUE, administered for the Utah Division of Real Estate), 'Exam Day,' Qualifying Questions #5

question: What is the name of Utah's standardized, state-approved form used for residential real estate purchase transactions, specifically identified in the exam content outline?
explanation: The exam content outline lists the Real Estate Purchase Contract (REPC) as a state-approved form under the 'Use of approved forms' topic, alongside other standardized forms used by Utah licensees.
source_note: Utah Real Estate State Broker Licensing Examination Content Outline, effective July 15, 2016, Section III.E 'Use of approved forms — Real Estate Purchase Contract (REPC)'

question: According to the official Utah broker exam content outline, what are the three recognized types of agency relationships in Utah real estate practice?
explanation: The content outline's Agency topic lists 'Types of Agency: Buyer, Seller, Limited' — notably using 'Limited' agency rather than the term 'dual agency' commonly used in other states.
source_note: Utah Real Estate State Broker Licensing Examination Content Outline, effective July 15, 2016, Section III.H 'Agency — 1. Types of Agency: Buyer, Seller, Limited'

question: Besides the types of agency recognized in Utah, what other agency-related topic is separately tested under the exam outline's 'Agency' category?
explanation: The Agency category of the content outline covers both the Types of Agency (Buyer, Seller, Limited) and Exclusive Brokerage Agreements as a distinct subtopic.
source_note: Utah Real Estate State Broker Licensing Examination Content Outline, effective July 15, 2016, Section III.H 'Agency — 2. Exclusive Brokerage Agreements'

question: Under the 'Role of the broker' topic in the Utah broker exam content outline, which two specific responsibilities are called out by name?
choice_d: MLS data entry and lockbox management
explanation: The content outline breaks 'Role of the broker' into two named components: (1) Supervision and (2) Trust accounts — reflecting the principal broker's core statutory duties to oversee affiliated licensees and safeguard client funds.
source_note: Utah Real Estate State Broker Licensing Examination Content Outline, effective July 15, 2016, Section III.F 'Role of the broker — 1. Supervision; 2. Trust accounts'

question: A candidate who passes the Utah real estate exam must also complete a fingerprinting process before a license will be issued. Which statement about this requirement is accurate?
choice_a: Fingerprinting is optional and only recommended for candidates seeking a broker license
choice_b: Digital fingerprinting is available at select Utah test centers for sales candidates, and the resulting receipt must be submitted with the license application
choice_c: Fingerprinting is handled entirely by the candidate's future employing broker, with no Division involvement
choice_d: Fingerprinting is required only for candidates who answer 'yes' to any background question
explanation: Candidates who pass the exam are required to complete fingerprinting; digital fingerprinting services are available for sales candidates at the Bountiful, Draper, Ogden, and Orem test centers, and the fingerprint receipt (or completed fingerprint cards, where digital service isn't offered) must be submitted with the license application to the Division.
source_note: Utah Real Estate Candidate Handbook (Pearson VUE, administered for the Utah Division of Real Estate), 'State Licensing Requirements,' Requirement I: Fingerprinting Requirement, and 'Exam Day,' Score Reporting

question: How does the application process for a Utah broker license differ from that for a sales agent license, according to the candidate handbook's licensing requirements?
choice_a: Broker applicants are exempt from the fingerprinting requirement
choice_b: Broker applicants do not need to pass any examination
choice_c: Broker applicants must additionally submit required documentation to the Division that is not required of sales agent applicants
choice_d: Broker applicants have no application deadline after passing the exam
explanation: The handbook sets out a separate 'Broker Applicant Requirements' provision stating that applicants applying for a broker license must submit additional required documentation to the Division, with detailed information and forms available at the Division's website.
source_note: Utah Real Estate Candidate Handbook (Pearson VUE, administered for the Utah Division of Real Estate), 'State Licensing Requirements,' Requirement H: Broker Applicant Requirements

question: Under Utah Code § 61-2f-201 (License required -- Scope of license), which three license types does a person generally need in order to lawfully engage in, or act in the capacity of, a real estate broker or agent in Utah?
choice_b: Managing Broker, Branch Broker, and Salesperson
choice_c: Qualifying Broker, Designated Broker, and Associate
choice_d: Principal Broker, Associate Broker, and Sales Agent
explanation: Section 61-2f-201 makes it unlawful for an unlicensed person to engage in the business of, act in the capacity of, or advertise as a 'principal broker, associate broker, or sales agent' with respect to real estate in Utah — the statute's three core license types.
source_note: Utah Code § 61-2f-201, 'License required -- Scope of license' (le.utah.gov, version effective 5/6/2026)

question: Utah Code § 61-2f-203 directs the Division of Real Estate to create an educational program for a newly created license type taking effect January 1, 2027. What is that license type, and how many hours of training must the program require at minimum?
explanation: Section 61-2f-203 requires the Division to create an educational program for a property manager license, effective on or after January 1, 2027, requiring at least 24 hours of training and covering subjects the Division determines necessary.
source_note: Utah Code § 61-2f-203, 'Licensing requirements' (le.utah.gov, version effective 5/6/2026)

question: For purposes of Utah's real estate prelicensing and continuing education requirements under Utah Code § 61-2f-203, how is one required 'hour' of instruction defined?
choice_a: 60 minutes of instruction in each 60-minute clock hour
choice_b: 50 minutes of instruction in each 60-minute clock hour
choice_c: 45 minutes of instruction in each 50-minute clock hour
choice_d: 40 minutes of instruction in each 60-minute clock hour
explanation: Section 61-2f-203 specifies that an hour required under the section 'means 50 minutes of instruction in each 60 minutes' — the standard classroom-hour definition used for prelicensing and continuing education programs.
source_note: Utah Code § 61-2f-203, 'Licensing requirements' (le.utah.gov, version effective 5/6/2026)

question: Under Utah Code § 61-2f-203, what is the maximum number of educational program hours that may be made available to a single individual in one day?
explanation: Section 61-2f-203 caps the maximum number of program hours available to an individual at eight hours per day.
source_note: Utah Code § 61-2f-203, 'Licensing requirements' (le.utah.gov, version effective 5/6/2026)

question: Per Utah Code § 61-2f-204 (Licensing fees and procedures -- Renewal fees and procedures), for what minimum period must the Division of Real Estate issue a real estate license (principal broker, associate broker, sales agent, or property manager)?
explanation: Section 61-2f-204 requires the Division to issue a license for a period of not less than two years, as the Division determines with the concurrence of the Commission.
source_note: Utah Code § 61-2f-204, 'Licensing fees and procedures -- Renewal fees and procedures' (le.utah.gov, version effective 5/6/2026)

question: As a condition of renewing an active Utah real estate license, Utah Code § 61-2f-204 requires a licensee to complete how many hours of continuing education within each two-year renewal period?
explanation: Section 61-2f-204 requires an active licensee, as a condition of renewal, to demonstrate competence by completing 18 hours of continuing education within a two-year renewal period, subject to rules made by the Commission with the concurrence of the Division.
source_note: Utah Code § 61-2f-204, 'Licensing fees and procedures -- Renewal fees and procedures' (le.utah.gov, version effective 5/6/2026)

question: If a Utah real estate license expires because it was not timely renewed, Utah Code § 61-2f-204 allows the Division to reinstate the license for how long after the expiration date, upon payment of a renewal fee and a late fee?
explanation: Section 61-2f-204 gives the Division a 30-day window after a license's expiration during which it may reinstate the license upon payment of a renewal fee and a late fee (the specific fee depending on whether the license was active or inactive when it expired).
source_note: Utah Code § 61-2f-204, 'Licensing fees and procedures -- Renewal fees and procedures' (le.utah.gov, version effective 5/6/2026)

question: Under Utah Code § 61-2f-204, if a Utah real estate license is revoked (or a revocation is upheld after a hearing), how soon may that individual apply for a new license?
choice_b: Not until at least 6 months after the revocation
choice_c: Not until at least 12 months after the revocation
choice_d: Never; revocation under this section is always permanent
explanation: Section 61-2f-204 provides that if a license is revoked, or a revocation is upheld after a hearing, the individual may not apply for a new license until at least 12 months after the day the license was revoked.
source_note: Utah Code § 61-2f-204, 'Licensing fees and procedures -- Renewal fees and procedures' (le.utah.gov, version effective 5/6/2026)

question: Utah Code § 61-2f-203 authorizes the Division, with Commission concurrence, to do which of the following regarding licensees from other states?
choice_a: Automatically issue a Utah license to any out-of-state licensee upon request
choice_b: Categorically bar all out-of-state applicants from Utah licensure
choice_c: Require out-of-state licensees to relicense only by completing a Utah law school program
choice_d: Enter into a reciprocal licensing agreement with another jurisdiction whose licensing requirements and standards are substantially similar to Utah's
explanation: Section 61-2f-203 permits the Division, with Commission concurrence, to enter into a reciprocal licensing agreement with another jurisdiction for licensure of a principal broker, associate broker, or sales agent, if that jurisdiction's requirements and standards are substantially similar to Utah's.
source_note: Utah Code § 61-2f-203, 'Licensing requirements' (le.utah.gov, version effective 5/6/2026)

question: Under Utah Code § 61-2f-203, a person who is not a Utah resident may be licensed as an associate broker or sales agent in Utah by complying with the chapter and doing what else?
choice_a: Being employed or engaged as an independent contractor by a principal broker who is licensed in Utah
choice_b: Maintaining a physical office address within Utah
choice_c: Passing only the national (non-state) portion of the exam
choice_d: Obtaining a letter of recommendation from the Utah Real Estate Commission chair
explanation: Section 61-2f-203 allows a nonresident to be licensed as an associate broker or sales agent in Utah by complying with the chapter and being employed or engaged as an independent contractor by or on behalf of a principal broker licensed in Utah, regardless of whether that principal broker is a Utah resident.
source_note: Utah Code § 61-2f-203, 'Licensing requirements' (le.utah.gov, version effective 5/6/2026)

question: If a person's Utah real estate license is revoked and the person later applies for a new principal broker or associate broker license, what does Utah Code § 61-2f-203 say about how that new application is treated?
choice_a: It is treated as a renewal, preserving the applicant's prior license number
choice_b: It is treated as an original application, and the applicant is not entitled to credit for experience gained before the revocation
choice_c: It automatically qualifies for a shortened examination
choice_d: It must be approved or denied within 10 business days
explanation: Section 61-2f-203 requires the Division and Commission to treat an application to be relicensed by someone whose license was revoked as an original application, and specifically denies the applicant credit for experience gained before the revocation when applying for a new principal broker or associate broker license.
source_note: Utah Code § 61-2f-203, 'Licensing requirements' (le.utah.gov, version effective 5/6/2026)

question: Under Utah Code § 61-2f-204, to activate a Utah real estate license that was inactive at the time of the licensee's most recent renewal, the licensee must supply proof of which of the following?
choice_a: A signed affidavit of good moral character only
choice_b: A new criminal background check only, with no education component
choice_c: Either passing the applicable sales agent or principal broker exam within six months before applying to activate, or completing the continuing education hours that would have been required had the license been active
choice_d: Payment of double the standard renewal fee
explanation: Section 61-2f-204 conditions activation of a previously inactive license on proof of either (1) successful completion of the respective sales agent or principal broker licensing examination within six months before applying to activate, or (2) successful completion of the continuing education hours that would have been required had the license been on active status at the time of the licensee's most recent renewal.
source_note: Utah Code § 61-2f-204, 'Licensing fees and procedures -- Renewal fees and procedures' (le.utah.gov, version effective 5/6/2026)

question: Under Utah Code § 61-2f-206 (Registration of person or branch office), what must a principal broker do regarding a location where the principal broker's brokerage operates apart from its main office?
choice_a: Nothing; only the main office must ever be registered
choice_b: Obtain a wholly separate principal broker license for each branch location
choice_c: File a branch notice only if the branch is located outside Utah
choice_d: Register each such branch office with the Division
explanation: Section 61-2f-206 requires a principal broker to register with the Division each of the principal broker's branch offices, in addition to registering the brokerage itself.
source_note: Utah Code § 61-2f-206, 'Registration of person or branch office -- Certification of education providers and courses -- Specialized licenses' (le.utah.gov, version effective 1/1/2026)

question: Except as otherwise provided by the Real Estate Licensing and Practices Act or by Commission rule, Utah Code § 61-2f-206 limits a principal broker to being responsible for how many registered entities at the same time?
explanation: Section 61-2f-206 provides that, except as otherwise provided under the chapter or by Commission rule, a principal broker may not be responsible for more than one registered entity at the same time.
source_note: Utah Code § 61-2f-206, 'Registration of person or branch office -- Certification of education providers and courses -- Specialized licenses' (le.utah.gov, version effective 1/1/2026)

question: Under Utah Code § 61-2f-206, what may a principal broker do to ensure active and reasonable supervision of a branch office while also supervising the main office?
choice_a: Close the branch office until the principal broker becomes personally available
choice_b: Designate a branch broker to supervise the branch office
choice_c: Delegate all supervisory duties entirely to the Division of Real Estate
choice_d: Rely on the branch office's sales agents to self-supervise with no broker oversight
explanation: Section 61-2f-206 allows a principal broker to designate a branch broker to supervise a branch office affiliated with the principal broker, while the principal broker exercises active and reasonable supervision of the main office; the branch broker must likewise exercise active and reasonable supervision of the branch office.
source_note: Utah Code § 61-2f-206, 'Registration of person or branch office -- Certification of education providers and courses -- Specialized licenses' (le.utah.gov, version effective 1/1/2026)
